shortDefinition: A way of organizing software where one program (the client) requests services from another program (the server).
analogy: Like a restaurant: the customer (client) orders food, and the kitchen (server) prepares and delivers it. The customer never needs to know how the kitchen works — they just place orders and get results.

blocks.content: The client-server model splits an application into two roles. The **client** asks for something; the **server** does the work and answers. The client is whatever the user holds — a browser, a phone app, a desktop program. The [[glossary:server|server]] is a program running somewhere central that waits for requests and responds to them. Crucially, the two only ever talk through a defined **request/response** exchange: the client sends a message describing what it wants, the server sends back a result. Neither side reaches into the other's internals.

A single round trip usually looks like this:

- The client opens a connection to the server's address.
- It sends a **request** — "give me this page," "create this order."
- The server processes it, often touching a [[glossary:database|database]] or other services.
- It sends back a **response** with the result (or an error).

The same server typically handles many clients at once, and any client can talk to any server that speaks the same protocol.

The model exists to put the **heavy, shared, or sensitive work in one place** instead of duplicating it on every user's device. The real data, the business rules, and the security checks all live on the server, where you control them. Clients stay thin: they render a screen and send requests. That's why you can fix a bug or change a price once, on the server, and every client sees it instantly without anyone installing an update.

Without this split, every device would need its own full copy of the data and logic — and keeping millions of copies in sync would be impossible. Centralizing on the server is what makes a shared, always-current application feasible at all.

Centralizing creates a dependency: the client can do little useful work when it can't reach the server. Every meaningful action becomes a network round trip, which adds latency and means the system must handle flaky connections, slow responses, and partial failures.

Two more costs come with the territory:

- **The server is a target.** Because everyone funnels through it, it must be scaled, secured, and kept available — it can become a bottleneck or a single point of failure.
- **Round trips add up.** A chatty client that makes many small requests feels slow; designing efficient requests matters.

Never trust the client. Anything running on the user's device can be inspected and tampered with, so validation, authorization, and pricing must be enforced on the server. Client-side checks are a convenience, not a security boundary.

Client-server is the backdrop for almost everything else in system design. The thing answering requests is a [[glossary:server|server]]; once you run more than one of them, a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] sits in front to spread requests across the pool. To keep any server able to handle any request, you push [[glossary:state|state]] out of the server and into a shared store, which in turn relies on a [[glossary:database|database]] for durable data.

The basic request/response shape also has variations. When a client needs updates the server can't predict, it may resort to [[glossary:polling|polling]] (asking repeatedly) or upgrade to [[glossary:websockets|websockets]] for a two-way connection — both are answers to the limits of one-shot request/response.

The web is the canonical example: your browser (client) sends **HTTP** requests to web servers, which respond with pages and data. Mobile apps work the same way, calling **REST** or **GraphQL** APIs over HTTP. The pattern shows up far beyond the web too — your email app is a client to a mail server, a SQL tool is a client to a database server, and a game client talks to game servers. Anywhere one program asks another for a service across a boundary, you're looking at client-server.

quiz.scenario: You're building a shopping app. A developer suggests storing the full product catalog and the discount rules inside the mobile app itself so it runs faster and works offline, with prices calculated on the device.
quiz.question: Why is computing the final price on the device the wrong call?

options.text: Pricing and other trusted logic belong on the server, because anything on the client can be inspected and tampered with.
options.explanation: This is the heart of the client-server model: keep sensitive, authoritative logic on the server you control. A device can be modified, so client-computed prices can't be trusted and would also drift out of sync the moment prices change.

options.text: Mobile devices don't have enough memory to hold a product catalog.
options.explanation: Modern phones can easily cache a catalog; size isn't the real issue. The problem is trust and keeping data current, not storage capacity.

options.text: Calculating a price is too CPU-intensive for a phone.
options.explanation: Arithmetic for pricing is trivial for any device. The concern is that the client is untrusted and can be manipulated, not that the math is heavy.

options.text: Offline support always causes data corruption.
options.explanation: Offline support is a legitimate feature, not an automatic source of corruption. The actual issue is enforcing authoritative pricing on the server rather than the client.

shortDefinition: A computer (or program) that receives requests from clients and sends back responses. It runs 24/7 so your app is always available.
analogy: Think of a server as a restaurant kitchen that never closes. Orders come in from customers all over the world, and the kitchen processes them and sends back results. The kitchen doesn't care who's ordering — it just handles requests.

blocks.content: A server is a long-running program that does one thing in a loop: **wait for a request, handle it, send a response, repeat** — for many clients at once. It listens on a network address and port, and when a request arrives it runs your application code, often reading or writing a [[glossary:database|database]] or calling other services, then returns a result. Unlike a program you launch and close, a server is meant to stay up indefinitely so the application is always reachable.

"Server" can mean the *machine* or the *program* — usually it's the program, and several can run on one machine. To serve many users simultaneously, a server handles requests concurrently (via multiple processes, threads, or an event loop). A key design choice is whether it is **stateless** or **stateful**:

- **Stateless** — the server keeps nothing about a client between requests; everything it needs comes in the request or from a shared store.
- **Stateful** — the server remembers something locally between requests, like a session in its own memory.

blocks.label: Why "stateless" is the goal
blocks.content: If a server stores no per-client memory of its own, then any server in the pool can handle any request. That means you can add, remove, or restart servers freely, and a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] can send a user's requests to whichever server is free. The moment a server holds [[glossary:state|state]] locally, requests get tied to a specific machine — and that machine dying loses the data.

The server is where your application actually *lives*. It's the one place that holds the trusted logic, talks to the database, and stays online so clients have something to talk to around the clock. Clients come and go; the server is the always-on hub that makes a shared application possible.

Keep servers **stateless** whenever you can. Stateless servers are interchangeable, which is what lets you scale out, deploy with zero downtime, and recover from a dead machine by simply routing around it.

A single server has a hard ceiling — only so much CPU, memory, and so many open connections — and it's a single point of failure: if it goes down, the application goes with it. The first response is usually a bigger machine ([[glossary:vertical-scaling|vertical scaling]]), but that ceiling arrives fast and still leaves you with one machine.

Running servers well takes ongoing effort: you have to monitor them, patch them, deploy new code without dropping requests, and plan for the moment one crashes. And a server that quietly accumulates local state is harder to scale and riskier to lose.

Storing session data in a server's own memory is a classic trap. It works with one server, but the moment you add a second one behind a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]], users get bounced to a server that's never heard of them. Put session state in a shared store, not in the server's local memory.

A server is one half of the [[glossary:client-server|client-server]] model — the half that answers. To grow past one machine you run several identical servers and put a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] in front, which is [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]] in action. Doing that cleanly depends on keeping servers stateless: persistent data goes to a [[glossary:database|database]], and transient session [[glossary:state|state]] goes to a shared [[glossary:in-memory-store|in-memory store]].

Running many servers also brings reliability tooling into play: [[glossary:health-check|health checks]] tell the load balancer which servers are alive, and [[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]] ensures the loss of one server doesn't take the system down.

In practice a "server" is your application running on top of a web server or runtime — **NGINX** or **Apache** fronting an app, or a process built with **Node.js**, **Django**, **Spring**, **Rails**, or **Go**. These run on virtual machines (**AWS EC2**, **Google Compute Engine**) or in containers orchestrated by **Kubernetes**. Increasingly, **serverless** platforms like **AWS Lambda** take the idea further: you supply just the request-handling code and the platform spins server capacity up and down for you — which only works cleanly because those functions are stateless by design.

quiz.scenario: Your app runs on a single server that stores each logged-in user's session in its own local memory. Traffic is growing, so you add a second identical server behind a load balancer. Suddenly users report being randomly logged out as they click around.
quiz.question: What's the root cause and the right fix?

options.text: Sessions live in one server's local memory; move session state to a shared store so any server can handle any request.
options.explanation: The servers are stateful, so the load balancer routes a user to a second server that has no record of their session. Making servers stateless by putting sessions in a shared store fixes it and lets you scale freely.

options.text: The load balancer is misconfigured; switch it to send all traffic to a single server.
options.explanation: That just undoes your scaling and recreates the original single-server bottleneck. The real issue is that session state is trapped in local server memory.

options.text: The database can't handle two servers connecting at once; add a read replica.
options.explanation: Databases routinely serve many servers, and read replicas address read load, not lost sessions. The logouts come from per-server local state, not the database.

options.text: The second server needs more memory to hold all the sessions.
options.explanation: More memory doesn't help, because each server still only knows its own sessions. The data needs to be shared across servers, not made larger on one.

shortDefinition: A system for storing and retrieving data permanently. Unlike memory (RAM), data in a database survives restarts and crashes.
analogy: A database is like a library's filing system. Every piece of data has a specific shelf and label so you can always find it again — even years later. Memory (RAM) is more like a sticky note: fast to read, but lost as soon as you clean up.

blocks.content: A database is a system dedicated to **storing data durably and finding it again efficiently**. At its core it writes your data to disk so it survives restarts and crashes, and it organizes that data so lookups don't require scanning everything. You don't read the raw files yourself — you ask the database through a query, and it does the work of locating, filtering, and returning the right records.

A few mechanisms make a database more than "files on disk":

- **Structured storage** — data is laid out in a defined shape (tables, documents, key-value pairs) so it can be queried, not just stored.
- **Indexes** — extra lookup structures, like a book's index, so the database can jump to the right rows instead of reading every one (see [[glossary:index|index]]).
- **Transactions** — a way to group several changes so they all happen or none do, keeping data consistent even if something fails midway.
- **Concurrency control** — rules that let many clients read and write at once without corrupting each other's data.

Memory (RAM) is fast but **forgotten the instant a program stops**. A database is what gives your application a memory that outlives any single request, restart, or crash — the difference between an order that's safely recorded and one that vanishes when the server reboots. It's the system's source of truth.

Almost every other piece of a system — caches, replicas, search indexes — is a faster or more convenient *copy* of what's in the database. The database is the original; everything else is derived from it, which is why getting it right matters most.

Durability has a price: writing to disk and guaranteeing consistency is far slower than touching memory. A database is often the **slowest, hardest-to-scale part** of a system — you can spin up more stateless app servers easily, but the one authoritative database is much harder to grow.

Choosing a database also means committing to trade-offs:

- **Speed vs. guarantees** — strict correctness (every read sees the latest write) costs performance.
- **Scaling is hard** — splitting or replicating a database to handle more load adds real complexity (see [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] and [[glossary:read-replica|read replicas]]).
- **It's the precious part** — losing app servers is annoying; losing the database is catastrophic, so backups and recovery are non-negotiable.

Don't treat a database like a cache. Hammering it with the same repeated reads, or storing throwaway session data in it, wastes its most precious resource. Use it for the durable source of truth and put a faster layer in front for hot reads.

The database is the durable backbone of the [[glossary:client-server|client-server]] model — the place a [[glossary:server|server]] turns to when it needs data that must survive. Because the database is slow and precious, several other concepts exist to protect it: a [[glossary:cache|cache]] absorbs repeated reads so they never reach it, [[glossary:read-replica|read replicas]] copy it to spread read load, and [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] splits it across machines when one can't hold everything.

It's also where [[glossary:persistence|persistence]] becomes concrete and where [[glossary:consistency|consistency]] choices get made — how strictly the database guarantees that everyone sees the same, latest data. The most common kind, the [[glossary:relational-database|relational database]], adds tables and relationships on top of these fundamentals.

Databases come in families suited to different shapes of data. **Relational (SQL)** systems like **PostgreSQL** and **MySQL** are the default for structured, related data with strong guarantees. **Document** stores like **MongoDB** hold flexible JSON-like records; **key-value** stores like **DynamoDB** and **Redis** trade richness for raw speed; **wide-column** stores like **Cassandra** handle enormous write volumes. Most real systems run more than one — a relational database as the source of truth, plus specialized stores for caching, search, or analytics alongside it.

quiz.scenario: Your team is prototyping a payments feature. To keep things fast, someone proposes keeping recorded payments only in the application server's memory while the app is running, and writing them to disk "later, in a batch."
quiz.question: What's the core problem with that approach?

options.text: Payments must be stored in a database so they survive a crash or restart; data held only in memory is lost the moment the process stops.
options.explanation: A database exists precisely to make data durable — the source of truth that outlives any restart. Payment records can't live only in volatile memory, where a crash before the batch write would silently destroy them.

options.text: In-memory storage is too slow for payments, so a database would be faster.
options.explanation: Memory is actually faster than a database, not slower. The issue isn't speed; it's that memory isn't durable, so committed payments could disappear.

options.text: Application servers aren't allowed to hold any data in memory.
options.explanation: Servers hold data in memory all the time for transient work. The real problem is relying on memory for data that must be permanent and survive failures.

options.text: A cache should be used to store the payments instead.
options.explanation: A cache is also volatile and meant for disposable copies of data, not the durable record. Payments need the persistent source of truth a database provides.

shortDefinition: A database that stores data in tables (rows and columns) with defined relationships between them. Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL.
analogy: Like a well-organized spreadsheet where each sheet represents a type of data (users, messages, chat rooms), and you can link rows across sheets. 'Show me all messages sent by user #42 in the general chat room' — a relational database handles that naturally.

blocks.content: A relational database stores data in **tables** — rows and columns, like spreadsheets. Each table holds one kind of thing (users, orders, products), each row is one record, and each column is a field with a defined type. What makes it *relational* is that rows in one table can reference rows in another through **keys**: an order row carries the `user_id` of the customer who placed it, linking the two tables. The database enforces a **schema** — the agreed structure — so every row in a table has the same shape.

You work with it through **SQL**, a declarative query language where you describe *what* you want and the database figures out *how* to get it. SQL's superpower is the **join**: combining related tables on the fly, like "every order, with the name of the customer who placed it." Two properties make this trustworthy:

- **ACID transactions** — Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable. A group of changes either all succeed or all roll back, and committed data survives crashes.
- **Constraints** — rules like "this field can't be empty" or "this `user_id` must point to a real user," enforced by the database itself.

blocks.label: What does ACID actually guarantee?
blocks.content: **Atomicity** — a transaction is all-or-nothing. **Consistency** — it moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting all constraints. **Isolation** — concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. **Durability** — once committed, the change survives even a power loss. Together they're why a bank transfer can debit one account and credit another without ever leaving money in limbo.

When your data is **interconnected** and **correctness is non-negotiable**, a relational database is the safest home for it. Money, inventory, bookings, and user accounts all need guarantees that two operations won't corrupt each other and that a half-finished change never sticks. ACID transactions provide exactly that, and the schema keeps bad or malformed data out before it ever lands.

When in doubt, start with a relational database. Its guarantees, mature tooling, and flexibility cover the vast majority of applications — reach for something more exotic only when you have a specific reason the relational model can't meet.

The structure that gives you safety also imposes rigidity. The schema must be defined up front and changing it later (a *migration*) takes care, especially on a large live table. Data that's genuinely unstructured or wildly variable can feel awkward to force into fixed columns.

The harder trade-off shows up at scale:

- **Hard to scale horizontally** — the joins and ACID guarantees that make relational databases great assume the data lives together on one machine. Splitting it across servers ([[glossary:sharding|sharding]]) breaks cross-machine joins and transactions.
- **Write throughput has a ceiling** — a single relational primary can only absorb so many writes before you must scale it the hard way.

Don't assume "relational" means "won't scale." A single well-tuned PostgreSQL or MySQL instance handles enormous load, and most apps never outgrow one. The classic mistake is reaching for a NoSQL store "for scale" you don't have, and giving up transactions and joins you actually need.

A relational database is the most common kind of [[glossary:database|database]], and it's where the abstract idea of [[glossary:persistence|persistence]] gets concrete tables and guarantees. It leans on [[glossary:index|indexes]] to keep queries fast as tables grow, and it offers [[glossary:strong-consistency|strong consistency]] by default — every read sees the latest committed write.

Its scaling path also defines several other concepts by contrast. You add [[glossary:read-replica|read replicas]] to spread read load, put a [[glossary:cache|cache]] in front to absorb hot reads, and only resort to [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] when one machine truly can't hold the data — each a way to relieve the database without giving up its core guarantees.

**PostgreSQL** and **MySQL** are the dominant open-source choices, with **SQLite** powering countless apps and devices and commercial systems like **Oracle** and **SQL Server** in the enterprise. Managed cloud versions — **Amazon RDS**, **Aurora**, **Google Cloud SQL** — handle backups, replicas, and failover for you. Newer **NewSQL** systems like **CockroachDB** and **Google Spanner** keep SQL and ACID guarantees while distributing data across many machines, chipping away at the old "relational can't scale" limitation.

quiz.scenario: You're designing a bank's money-transfer feature. Each transfer must debit one account and credit another, and under no circumstances can money be debited without the matching credit succeeding — even if the server crashes mid-operation.
quiz.question: Which storage choice best fits this requirement?

options.text: A relational database, wrapping the debit and credit in a single ACID transaction.
options.explanation: This is exactly what ACID transactions are for: the debit and credit are atomic — both happen or neither does — and durable once committed. A relational database guarantees money never gets stuck in limbo, even through a crash.

options.text: An in-memory store like Redis for maximum speed.
options.explanation: An in-memory store is fast but volatile and not built for multi-step financial atomicity. A crash could lose committed transfers — unacceptable for money.

options.text: A document store, saving each account balance as a JSON document.
options.explanation: Document stores often lack strong multi-record transactions across separate accounts, making it hard to guarantee the debit and credit always succeed or fail together. Relational ACID transactions handle this directly.

options.text: A cache in front of plain files on disk.
options.explanation: A cache holds disposable copies and offers no transactional guarantees, and raw files give you no atomicity or constraints. Neither protects against a partial transfer the way an ACID database does.

shortDefinition: Storing data so it survives beyond the current session. Persistent data doesn't disappear when the program stops.
analogy: The difference between writing on a whiteboard (non-persistent — erased at end of day) and writing in a notebook (persistent — stays there until you choose to erase it).

blocks.content: Persistence means writing data to **durable storage** — disk, SSD, or another medium that keeps its contents when the power is off — so the data survives beyond the moment your program is running. The opposite is **volatile** storage like RAM, which is fast but wiped clean the instant a process stops or a machine restarts. To persist something is to commit it somewhere it will still be there tomorrow.

The dividing line is simple:

- **Volatile (RAM)** — extremely fast, but its contents vanish on restart, crash, or power loss. Good for in-flight work and disposable copies.
- **Persistent (disk/SSD)** — slower to read and write, but its contents endure. Good for anything you can't afford to lose.

Making a write *truly* persistent usually means forcing it all the way to disk (a `flush` or `fsync`), because operating systems and disks buffer writes in memory first for speed — and that buffer is not yet safe.

Persistence is the difference between an application that *remembers* and one that forgets everything the moment it hiccups. A user's account, their order history, an uploaded photo — none of that can live only in memory, because servers restart, crash, and get redeployed constantly. Persistence is what lets a system survive its own inevitable interruptions without losing what matters.

Servers are disposable; data is not. The whole reason we tolerate the slowness of disk is that some things simply must outlive the program that created them. Deciding *what* must persist is one of the first design questions for any system.

Durability costs speed. Writing to disk and confirming it's really there is far slower than touching RAM — often by orders of magnitude. Persisting everything would make a system crawl, so the art is choosing what genuinely needs to survive and what can stay fast and volatile.

There's also a spectrum, not a binary:

- **Persistent but lossy windows** — many systems buffer writes briefly for speed, so a crash can lose the last few seconds of "saved" data unless you force a flush.
- **Persistent isn't automatically safe** — a single disk can still fail. Real durability needs copies ([[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]]) and backups, not just one write to one drive.
- **More durable usually means slower** — synchronous, replicated writes are safest and least performant.

"It said it saved" is not the same as "it's safe." Confirming a write reached fast memory or a single disk's buffer can still lose data on a crash or hardware failure. Know whether your storage flushed to durable media and whether there's a second copy.

Persistence is the property a [[glossary:database|database]] is built to provide — its entire job is storing data so it survives. It's the defining contrast with an [[glossary:in-memory-store|in-memory store]] and a [[glossary:cache|cache]], both of which trade persistence for raw speed by keeping data in volatile RAM. And it's why [[glossary:state|state]] is tricky: deciding which state must persist and which can stay in memory is a core design call.

True durability also depends on [[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]] — keeping more than one copy — because a single persisted file is only as safe as the one disk it sits on. Persistence and replication together are what make data genuinely survivable.

Persistence shows up at every layer. Databases write to disk and keep a **write-ahead log** so an interrupted transaction can be recovered. Even normally-volatile stores can opt in: **Redis** offers snapshots (RDB) and an append-only log (AOF) to persist its in-memory data. At the infrastructure level, **block storage** (AWS EBS), **object storage** (S3), and replicated filesystems provide durable homes for data, often keeping multiple copies automatically so a single disk failure never means data loss.

quiz.scenario: A teammate reports that user uploads occasionally vanish after a deploy. Investigating, you find the app saves uploaded files into a temporary folder on the application server's local disk, and deploys replace the server with a fresh one.
quiz.question: What's the underlying problem?

options.text: The uploads aren't truly persisted to durable, independent storage, so they're lost when the disposable server is replaced.
options.explanation: Persistence means data must survive beyond the lifetime of the program and machine that created it. A temp folder on a server that gets thrown away on every deploy isn't durable storage — the files need to live somewhere independent and lasting.

options.text: The server doesn't have enough disk space, so old uploads get overwritten.
options.explanation: The files disappear on deploy, not when disk fills up. The issue is that they live on a disposable server rather than in persistent storage.

options.text: The uploads should be cached in memory for faster access.
options.explanation: Caching in memory is even more volatile and would lose the files just as readily. The fix is durable storage, not a faster volatile copy.

options.text: The deploy process is too frequent; deploying less often would keep the files around.
options.explanation: Deploying less often only hides the bug between deploys. The data still isn't persisted, so it will vanish on the next deploy or crash regardless.

shortDefinition: A technique where a client repeatedly asks the server 'do you have anything new?' at regular intervals.
analogy: Like checking your mailbox every 5 minutes to see if anything arrived. Simple and reliable, but wastes a lot of trips when there's usually nothing there.

blocks.content: Polling is the simplest way for a client to stay up to date: it just **asks the server, over and over**, "anything new?" Each ask is an ordinary request — the same kind your browser makes to load any page — and the server answers with whatever it has, even if that answer is "nothing changed." The client waits a beat, then asks again.

There are two flavors, and the difference matters:

- **Short polling** — the client sends a request on a fixed timer (say, every 5 seconds). The server replies *immediately* with the current state, empty or not. Easy to build, but most requests come back empty.
- **Long polling** — the client sends a request and the server *holds it open* until it actually has something to send (or a timeout hits). The moment new data exists, the server responds and the client immediately opens a fresh request. This feels much closer to instant while still using plain requests.
If you're tempted to poll faster to feel more "live," reach for **long polling** first. It gives near-instant delivery without the flood of empty requests that aggressive short polling creates.

The web's default model is **request/response**: the client asks, the server answers, the conversation ends. That's perfect for loading a page, but it has no way for the server to say "hey, something happened" on its own. Polling is the oldest, most universal workaround — it fakes a live feed by asking again and again.

Its great virtue is that it needs *nothing special*. It runs over plain HTTP, works through every firewall and proxy, survives flaky connections, and is trivial to reason about. For data that updates slowly — a build status, an order's progress, a dashboard that refreshes every minute — polling is often the right answer precisely because it's boring and reliable.

Polling's weakness is **waste**. With short polling, most requests return nothing, yet each one still costs a round trip, a connection, and server work to answer. Multiply that by thousands of clients and you're spending real capacity to mostly say "nothing yet."

You're also stuck choosing between two bad extremes:

- **Poll often** — lower delay, but far more load and wasted requests.
- **Poll rarely** — cheaper, but users see stale data and updates feel sluggish.

Long polling eases the waste but ties up a server connection per waiting client, which can pile up under heavy load.

Don't crank the polling interval down to chase a truly live feel. Once you need sub-second updates for many users — chat, live cursors, gameplay — polling stops being the cheap option and you should switch to [[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]].

Polling is one of two classic ways to deliver [[glossary:real-time|real-time]] data, and it's the easy end of that spectrum. Its counterpart is [[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]]: where polling makes the *client* repeatedly ask, a WebSocket lets the *server* push the moment something changes. A good rule of thumb is to start with polling and graduate to WebSockets only when the update rate or user count makes the waste hurt.

Polling also shows up as the natural companion to [[glossary:async|asynchronous processing]]: when you hand off a long job to the background, polling a status endpoint ("is my report ready yet?") is a common, low-tech way to find out when it finishes.

blocks.caption: Without push, the client keeps asking — most answers are 'nothing new'.

blocks.content: Short polling is everywhere there's a status to check: CI dashboards, package-tracking pages, and `setInterval` calls hitting a REST endpoint from a browser. Long polling powered the first generation of live web apps — early Gmail chat and Facebook used it — and it still backs fallbacks in libraries like **Socket.IO**, which long-polls when a WebSocket can't be established. For one-way streams from server to client, **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** are a lighter modern alternative that keeps the simplicity of HTTP while letting the server push.

quiz.scenario: You're building a page that shows the status of a long-running export job. The job takes anywhere from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and you just need to update a progress label until it's done. You want the simplest thing that works over ordinary HTTP.
quiz.question: What's the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Have the client poll a status endpoint every few seconds until the job reports done.
options.explanation: This is polling's sweet spot: an occasional update, no need for sub-second latency, and nothing fancier than plain HTTP requests. Simple and reliable.

options.text: Open a WebSocket connection so the server can push progress.
options.explanation: A persistent bidirectional connection is overkill for an occasional status check. WebSockets shine for high-frequency, two-way updates — not a slow progress label.

options.text: Put the job behind a message queue and read from the queue in the browser.
options.explanation: A message queue decouples backend services; browsers don't consume queues directly. It doesn't solve the client-update problem here.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the status endpoint.
options.explanation: A cache would actually hurt — it could serve a stale status. The challenge is delivering fresh updates to the client, which caching doesn't address.

shortDefinition: A technology that creates a persistent, two-way connection between client and server. Either side can send data at any time without waiting for a request.
analogy: If HTTP (regular web requests) is like sending letters back and forth, WebSockets are like a phone call — once connected, both sides can talk whenever they want. No need to hang up and dial again for each message.

blocks.content: A WebSocket turns a normal web request into a **persistent, two-way pipe** between client and server. It starts life as an ordinary HTTP request carrying a special `Upgrade` header; if the server agrees, the connection is *upgraded* and stays open. From that point on, both sides can send messages whenever they like, in either direction, without the request-then-response dance of regular HTTP.

The two key properties to remember:

- **Persistent** — the connection is opened once and kept alive, instead of a fresh connection per message.
- **Bidirectional (full-duplex)** — the server can push to the client *and* the client can send to the server, at the same time, independently.

Because it's always open, the server can deliver an update the instant it happens — no waiting for the client to ask.

blocks.label: What keeps the connection alive?
blocks.content: Idle connections can be silently dropped by proxies or load balancers, so WebSockets use periodic **ping/pong** heartbeats — tiny control messages that prove both ends are still there. If a heartbeat goes unanswered, the connection is considered dead and the client typically reconnects.

Plain HTTP can't let a server speak first — it can only answer. That's a real problem for anything genuinely live, where the server needs to tell clients about changes *as they happen*. WebSockets close that gap: the server pushes, instantly, the moment there's something to say.

The deeper win is **efficiency at high frequency**. Compared with hammering a server through fast [[glossary:polling|polling]], one open WebSocket carries a stream of updates with almost no per-message overhead — no new connection, no repeated headers, no empty "nothing yet" replies.

Keeping connections open isn't free. Every connected client holds a live connection on the server, consuming memory and a slot in the connection table whether or not it's sending anything. A million idle users is a million open sockets to manage — a very different scaling profile from stateless requests.

Other costs to weigh:

- **Harder to scale horizontally** — a long-lived connection is a kind of [[glossary:state|state]], so a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] can't freely move a client between servers mid-connection.
- **Reconnection logic** — networks drop; clients must detect dead connections and re-establish them, often re-syncing missed data.
- **Infrastructure friction** — some proxies and older firewalls handle long-lived upgraded connections poorly.

Don't reach for WebSockets just because they sound modern. If your data updates occasionally or only flows one way, plain [[glossary:polling|polling]] or Server-Sent Events are simpler, cheaper, and far easier to scale. Pay for a persistent connection only when you genuinely need frequent, two-way, instant communication.

WebSockets are the heavy-duty tool for [[glossary:real-time|real-time]] features, sitting at the opposite end of the spectrum from [[glossary:polling|polling]]. Polling makes the client ask repeatedly; a WebSocket lets the server push. The usual progression is to begin with polling and adopt WebSockets once update frequency or interactivity demands it.

Because a WebSocket connection is long-lived [[glossary:state|state]] pinned to one server, it complicates the otherwise-clean story of [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancers]] and [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]]: you typically need sticky routing plus a shared backplane (often built on a [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]] or pub/sub layer) so a message produced on one server can reach a client connected to another.

blocks.caption: One persistent connection lets the server push the moment data changes.

blocks.content: WebSockets power chat apps (Slack, Discord), collaborative editors (Figma, Google Docs cursors), live trading and sports tickers, and multiplayer game state. **Socket.IO** is the popular JavaScript library that wraps WebSockets with reconnection and a polling fallback baked in. On the backend, managed services like **AWS API Gateway WebSockets**, **Pusher**, and **Ably** handle the hard parts of fan-out and connection management so you don't have to run the socket fleet yourself.

quiz.scenario: You're building a multiplayer drawing app where every user must see others' brush strokes appear instantly, and each user is also constantly sending their own strokes. There are many simultaneous users in a room, all updating several times per second.
quiz.question: Which technology fits best?

options.text: Open a WebSocket connection per client so the server can push strokes and receive them in real time.
options.explanation: High-frequency, bidirectional, instant updates between many clients is exactly what a persistent WebSocket connection is designed for.

options.text: Have each client short-poll the server several times per second.
options.explanation: Polling that fast floods the server with requests and still adds delay between strokes. It can't match the latency or efficiency of an open connection for this workload.

options.text: Use Server-Sent Events to stream strokes to clients.
options.explanation: SSE is one-way (server to client only). Here clients also need to send their strokes constantly, which SSE can't do — you'd need a second channel.

options.text: Put every stroke into a message queue and let clients drain it.
options.explanation: A message queue decouples backend services and isn't a client-facing transport. It doesn't give the browser a live, bidirectional channel to other users.

shortDefinition: Data that is delivered immediately as it's created, with no noticeable delay. Chat messages, live scores, and collaborative editing are all real-time features.
analogy: The difference between watching a live sports game (real-time) and reading the score in tomorrow's newspaper (batch). Real-time means you see it as it happens.

blocks.content: "Real-time" describes a *goal*, not a single technology: deliver data to users **as it happens**, with no delay they'd notice. In practice that means closing the gap between when something changes on the server and when the user sees it — ideally down to milliseconds.

Because plain HTTP only lets a server answer when asked, real-time features are built with techniques that work around that limit. The main three, from simplest to most capable:

- **[[glossary:polling|Polling]]** — the client repeatedly asks for updates. Easiest, but wasteful and laggy.
- **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** — the server streams updates one-way over a single open HTTP connection. Great for feeds and notifications.
- **[[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]]** — a persistent two-way connection, so either side can send instantly. The tool for truly interactive, high-frequency updates.

"Real-time" rarely means *zero* delay — it means *imperceptible* delay for the task at hand. A chat message within a second feels instant; a stock trade may need single-digit milliseconds. Define how fresh "fresh enough" is before picking a mechanism.

Some experiences simply don't work unless they're live. A chat where messages arrive a minute late isn't a chat. A collaborative document where you can't see a teammate's edits is just a document. Live scores, ride-tracking maps, trading screens, multiplayer games — their entire value is in the *immediacy*.

Without real-time delivery, you fall back to users manually refreshing or staring at stale data, never sure if what they're seeing is current. Real-time turns an app from a snapshot into a living view that keeps itself up to date.

Live data costs more than data on request. Keeping clients current means either constant asking ([[glossary:polling|polling]] overhead) or holding open connections ([[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]] and their per-client memory). Either way, real-time systems carry load even when nothing important is happening, and they're harder to scale than simple request/response.
There's also a temptation to make *everything* live. Most data doesn't need it — a settings page or a monthly report gains nothing from instant updates and pays the complexity cost for free.

Don't confuse "real-time" with "as fast as possible." Treating every feature as real-time bloats your infrastructure and your bugs. Reserve it for the handful of features where immediacy is the point, and let everything else use ordinary requests.

Real-time is the umbrella; [[glossary:polling|polling]] and [[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]] are the two main ways under it to actually achieve it. Polling fakes liveness by asking repeatedly and is the easy starting point; WebSockets deliver true server push and are the destination when updates get frequent or interactive.

It's worth contrasting real-time with [[glossary:async|asynchronous processing]], which can sound similar but is the opposite intent: async deliberately *delays* work to the background so the user doesn't wait, while real-time works to *eliminate* delay. Internally, real-time systems that fan one event out to many connected users often lean on an [[glossary:event-driven|event-driven]] backbone and a [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]] or pub/sub layer to route updates between servers.

Real-time shows up across familiar products: Slack and WhatsApp messaging, Google Docs co-editing, Uber's live driver map, live sports and election dashboards, and trading platforms. Under the hood you'll find WebSockets (often via **Socket.IO**), **SSE** for one-way feeds, and managed real-time platforms like **Pusher**, **Ably**, and **Firebase Realtime Database / Firestore** that handle connection fan-out and delivery so teams can ship live features without building the plumbing themselves.

quiz.scenario: A product team wants their dashboard to feel "real-time." Looking closer, the numbers on it come from a report that's recomputed once an hour, and users check it a few times a day. The team is debating which live-update technology to add.
quiz.question: What's the soundest decision?

options.text: Skip real-time delivery here — the data only changes hourly, so a refresh on load (or light polling) is plenty.
options.explanation: Real-time only earns its cost when immediacy matters. Hourly data viewed a few times a day gains nothing from live connections; the right call is to recognize this isn't a real-time problem at all.

options.text: Add WebSockets so the dashboard updates instantly.
options.explanation: Persistent connections are pure overhead when the underlying data only changes once an hour. You'd pay the scaling cost of WebSockets for no perceptible benefit.

options.text: Poll the server every second to keep it fresh.
options.explanation: Polling every second against data that changes hourly is almost entirely wasted requests. The update frequency doesn't justify it.

options.text: Stream updates with Server-Sent Events.
options.explanation: SSE is a fine real-time tool, but there's nothing real-time to deliver here. Holding a streaming connection open for hourly data is needless complexity.

shortDefinition: Loading data in small chunks instead of all at once. Show 50 items, then load the next 50 when needed.
analogy: Like a book divided into pages. You don't print the entire book on one giant scroll — you break it into manageable pages. Google search results (page 1, 2, 3) and Twitter's infinite scroll are both forms of pagination.

blocks.content: Pagination serves a large result set in small **pages** instead of all at once. The client asks for a slice — say, the first 50 items — and asks for the next slice only when it needs more. The server returns just that slice plus enough information to fetch the following one.

There are two main strategies, and the difference matters:

- **Offset-based** — `LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100` (“skip 100, give me the next 50”). Simple, supports jumping to any page, and is how numbered page links work. But the database still has to count past all the skipped rows, so deep pages get slow, and rows shifting can cause duplicates or skips.
- **Cursor-based (keyset)** — “give me 50 items *after* this one,” using a stable marker like an ID or timestamp (`WHERE id > last_seen_id LIMIT 50`). It jumps straight to the right spot with no counting, so it stays fast at any depth and is stable as data changes — but you can only move forward/back, not to an arbitrary page number.
**Infinite scroll** is just cursor-based pagination with a nicer coat of paint — each “load more” quietly fetches the next page after the last item you saw.

Returning an unbounded list is a trap. A query that fetches *all* matching rows might pull back millions — a huge load on the database, a huge payload over the network, and a browser asked to render far more than a person can read. Pagination caps that cost: the system only ever does the work for one page at a time.

It also keeps the experience **fast and predictable**. Users get the first page almost instantly instead of staring at a spinner while everything loads, and your server's memory and response times stay bounded no matter how big the underlying data set grows.

Any endpoint that returns a list should paginate — even ones that “only” return a few hundred rows today. Data grows, and an endpoint that returns *everything* is a latency and out-of-memory incident waiting to happen.

The catch is choosing the right strategy, and each has a real cost. **Offset** is easy and lets users jump to page 47, but it degrades on deep pages — `OFFSET 1000000` makes the database walk past a million rows — and it can show duplicates or gaps when items are added or removed while a user pages through. **Cursor** is fast and stable at any depth, but it can't jump to an arbitrary page and is a bit more work to implement.

Pick by access pattern: **offset** for small data sets where users want numbered pages; **cursor** for large, fast-changing feeds and infinite scroll where they only ever move forward. Whichever you choose, an [[glossary:index|index]] on the sort/cursor column is what keeps it fast.

Pagination is fundamentally about reading from a [[glossary:database|database]] efficiently, and it leans hard on an [[glossary:index|index]]: cursor pagination needs an index on the column it sorts and seeks by, or each page falls back to a slow scan. It also helps the whole stack — smaller responses are easier to [[glossary:cache|cache]] (a page is a stable, repeatable unit) and lighter on every hop between client and server.

On very large systems, pagination interacts with [[glossary:sharding|sharding]]: paging across a data set split over many shards is tricky, since a single page may need results gathered and merged from several shards — one reason cursor schemes are often designed shard-aware.

REST APIs commonly expose `?page=2&per_page=50` (offset) or `?cursor=abc123` (cursor) parameters. **GitHub** and **Stripe** use cursor-based pagination for their large, changing lists, returning a `next` cursor in each response. **GraphQL**'s Relay spec standardizes cursor pagination with `edges`, `nodes`, and `pageInfo`. SQL implements offset with `LIMIT ... OFFSET ...`; keyset pagination uses a `WHERE` clause on the last-seen value plus `ORDER BY` over an indexed column.

quiz.scenario: Your social app shows an activity feed that can hold hundreds of thousands of items per user. Loading the whole feed at once is slow and sometimes crashes the mobile app, and new items are constantly being added at the top.
quiz.question: What's the best way to serve the feed?

options.text: Paginate with a cursor, fetching the next batch of items after the last one the user saw.
options.explanation: A feed is large, constantly changing, and consumed by scrolling forward — the textbook case for cursor-based pagination. It stays fast at any depth and won't skip or duplicate items as new ones arrive at the top.

options.text: Use offset pagination with numbered pages (LIMIT/OFFSET).
options.explanation: Offset works for small, stable lists, but on a huge, fast-changing feed deep offsets get slow, and new items arriving at the top cause duplicates and skips between pages. Cursor pagination avoids both.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the feed query.
options.explanation: A cache might speed up repeated reads, but it doesn't shrink the response — you'd still be loading the entire enormous feed and crashing the app. The problem is fetching everything at once, which pagination fixes.

options.text: Move the database to a more powerful machine.
options.explanation: Vertical scaling makes the giant query a bit faster, but you're still transferring and rendering the whole feed. The fix is to load it in bounded chunks, not to throw hardware at an unbounded fetch.

shortDefinition: A temporary storage layer that keeps frequently accessed data close at hand so you don't have to fetch it from the original source every time. It trades freshness for speed.
analogy: Like keeping a cookbook on your kitchen counter instead of walking to the bookshelf every time you need a recipe. The counter has limited space, but anything on it is much faster to grab.

blocks.content: A cache sits **between** whatever is asking for data and the slow source of truth behind it. The first time a piece of data is requested, the system fetches it from the original source — a [[glossary:database|database]], an API, or disk — and stores a copy in fast memory. Every request after that is served from the copy. That's a **cache hit**. When the data isn't there, it's a **cache miss**, and the system pays the full cost of going to the source.

The most common arrangement is **cache-aside**: your application checks the cache first and, only on a miss, reads the source and writes the result back for next time. Two other patterns trade freshness for simplicity: **write-through** updates the cache and the source together on every write, while **write-back** updates the cache immediately and the source later. Three knobs control any cache:

- **TTL (time-to-live)** — how long a copy is allowed to live before it's considered stale.
- **Eviction policy** — what to drop when memory fills up. **LRU** (least-recently-used) is the usual default.
- **Hit ratio** — the share of requests served from cache. The whole point is to keep this high.

Reading from memory is **orders of magnitude faster** than reading from disk or crossing the network — microseconds instead of milliseconds. For data that's read far more often than it changes, a cache turns a slow, repeated lookup into an instant one.

Just as important, a cache **absorbs traffic**. In most systems a small slice of the data is requested constantly — the homepage, a trending product, a popular profile. Serving those from cache means your database only sees the requests that actually miss, so it can stay small and cheap while the app handles far more load.
Rule of thumb: cache data that is **read often and changes rarely**. The bigger the gap between read rate and write rate, the more a cache pays off.

A cache is a *copy*, and copies drift out of date. The central question is always: how stale is too stale? A short TTL keeps data fresh but lowers your hit ratio; a long TTL is faster but risks serving wrong answers. You're trading **freshness for speed**, and only your use case can say where the line is.

Caching also adds real costs:

- **Stale reads** — users may see out-of-date data until the copy expires.
- **Extra moving parts** — another system to run, size, and monitor.
- **Cold starts & stampedes** — right after a deploy or eviction, many misses can hit the database at once (a *thundering herd*).

There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Knowing **when** to throw away a stale copy is the part that bites teams — plan your invalidation strategy before you add the cache, not after.

A cache rarely lives alone — it's a layer that shows up at several points in a system. Closest to the user, a [[glossary:cdn|CDN]] is itself a cache for static files spread around the globe. Inside your system, a cache sits between the app and the [[glossary:database|database]], shielding it from repeated reads. It's usually backed by an [[glossary:in-memory-store|in-memory store]] like Redis, and it complements [[glossary:read-replica|read replicas]]: replicas scale out the database itself, while a cache avoids touching the database at all.

Caching is also where you confront [[glossary:consistency|consistency]] head-on. The moment you keep a copy, you accept that it can disagree with the source — so a cache is a deliberate choice to favor speed over perfectly fresh data.

blocks.caption: Cache-aside: the app checks the cache first and only reaches the database on a miss.

blocks.content: **Redis** and **Memcached** are the workhorses for application caches — fast key-value stores that sit beside your servers. At the edge, **CDNs** like Cloudflare and Fastly cache static assets, and browsers cache responses based on HTTP `Cache-Control` headers. Databases add their own layers too: query caches and buffer pools keep hot pages in memory. Most real systems stack several of these at once — browser, CDN, application cache, and database cache — each catching what the layer in front of it missed.

quiz.scenario: Your product-detail page reads the same item from the database on every visit, and an item's details change at most once a day. Under traffic, the database is becoming the bottleneck.
quiz.question: What's the most effective first move?

options.text: Put a cache in front of the database and serve item details from it with a short TTL.
options.explanation: Exactly the case caching is built for: data read constantly but changed rarely. The cache absorbs the repeated reads, and a short TTL keeps it fresh enough for once-a-day changes.

options.text: Shard the database by product ID.
options.explanation: Sharding helps when the data set is too big for one server. Here the problem is repeated reads of the same hot items — splitting the data does little for that.

options.text: Add more application servers behind the load balancer.
options.explanation: More app servers just send more queries to the same database. The bottleneck is the database read load, not application compute.

options.text: Switch the database to eventual consistency.
options.explanation: A consistency model changes how copies agree, not how many reads hit the database. It doesn't reduce the read load causing the bottleneck.

shortDefinition: A network of servers spread across the globe that stores copies of your content (images, videos, pages) closer to users. Instead of everyone fetching from one far-away server, they get it from a nearby one.
analogy: Like a franchise restaurant chain. Instead of one central kitchen shipping food worldwide, each city has its own location serving the same menu. Customers get their food faster because the kitchen is right around the corner.

blocks.content: A CDN is a fleet of servers — called **edge servers** or **points of presence (PoPs)** — scattered across cities and continents. Each edge server keeps cached copies of your content. When a user requests a file, they're routed to the *nearest* edge instead of your one **origin server**, so the data travels a short hop instead of crossing the planet.

The first time an edge is asked for a file it doesn't have, it fetches it from the origin, sends it to the user, and keeps a copy. Every later request from that region is served straight from the edge. A few knobs control the behavior:

- **TTL (time-to-live)** — how long an edge holds a copy before checking the origin for a fresher one.
- **Cache hit ratio** — the share of requests the edges serve without touching the origin. Higher is better.
- **Purge / invalidation** — how you force every edge to drop a stale copy when you ship a change.

Users are steered to the closest edge by **anycast routing** or smart DNS, which hands each user the address of a nearby PoP.

Distance is latency. Data can't travel faster than light, so a request that has to cross an ocean pays an unavoidable round-trip penalty no faster server can fix. By putting content a few milliseconds from the user, a CDN makes pages and media feel instant no matter where the visitor is.

A CDN also **shields your origin**. Static assets — images, videos, scripts, stylesheets — are usually the bulk of a site's traffic, and they rarely change. Letting the edges serve them means your origin handles only a thin slice of requests, so it stays small and cheap even under heavy global load.
Because the edge absorbs floods of traffic, a CDN is also your first line of defense against spikes and DDoS attacks — the surge slams the distributed edge network instead of your single origin.

A CDN is a cache spread across the world, so it inherits a cache's central problem: copies go stale. Push a new logo or a fixed script and old versions can linger at the edges until their TTL expires — different users may see different versions for a while. You manage this with **cache-busting** (changing the filename, e.g. `app.a1b2c3.js`) or by **purging** the edges on deploy.

Other costs to weigh:

- **Best for static, public content** — personalized or constantly-changing responses get few cache hits, so the CDN mostly just adds a hop.
- **Another vendor and bill** — one more system to configure, monitor, and pay for, usually by bandwidth.
- **Debugging gets murkier** — “why is this user seeing an old file?” often means hunting down which edge served a stale copy.

Don't put data behind a CDN with a long TTL and no invalidation plan. The classic incident is shipping a critical fix, only to have edges keep serving the broken version for hours because nobody set up cache-busting or a purge.

A CDN is fundamentally a [[glossary:cache|cache]] — the same trade of freshness for speed — but placed at the *edge*, closest to the user, rather than inside your data center. It sits in front of your origin [[glossary:server|servers]] and is a form of geographic [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]]: instead of one big origin, you spread copies across many locations.

It pairs naturally with a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] — the CDN handles static assets at the edge, while the load balancer spreads the dynamic requests that reach your origin across your application servers. Because edge copies can lag the origin, a CDN is another place you accept [[glossary:eventual-consistency|eventual consistency]]: every edge converges on the latest version once TTLs expire or you purge.

blocks.caption: Edge servers serve users from nearby; only a miss travels back to the origin.

blocks.content: **Cloudflare**, **Akamai**, **Fastly**, and **AWS CloudFront** are the major CDNs, with thousands of edge locations worldwide. They cache static files and increasingly run code at the edge too — **Cloudflare Workers** and **CloudFront Functions** let you personalize or rewrite responses near the user. Most sites serve images, video, fonts, and JavaScript bundles through a CDN by default, controlling behavior with HTTP `Cache-Control` headers and versioned filenames so a deploy invalidates the old assets cleanly.

quiz.scenario: Your app's origin server is in Virginia, but a growing share of users are in Europe and Asia. They complain that images and video load slowly, even though your servers aren't overloaded.
quiz.question: What's the most effective fix?

options.text: Serve the static assets through a CDN so users fetch them from a nearby edge location.
options.explanation: The problem is distance, not server load. A CDN caches the images and video at edge servers around the world, so each user gets them from a nearby PoP instead of crossing the ocean to Virginia.

options.text: Upgrade the origin server to a more powerful machine.
options.explanation: Vertical scaling makes the server faster, but it can't shorten the physical distance the data travels. A bigger machine in Virginia is still far from Asia.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the origin database.
options.explanation: An origin-side cache speeds up data lookups inside your data center, but users still have to reach Virginia to get the response. It doesn't reduce the cross-continent latency.

options.text: Put a load balancer in front of the origin.
options.explanation: A load balancer spreads requests across servers, which helps with load — but the servers aren't overloaded. It does nothing about the distance causing the slowness.

shortDefinition: A system that distributes incoming requests across multiple servers so no single server gets overwhelmed. It acts as a traffic director for your application.
analogy: Like a host at a busy restaurant who seats guests across all available tables instead of sending everyone to the same waiter. Each waiter handles a fair share, and the restaurant runs smoothly.

blocks.content: A load balancer is the **single front door** to a pool of identical servers. Clients connect to one address — the load balancer — and it decides, request by request, which server in the pool should handle each one. The servers behind it never talk to clients directly.

How it picks a server depends on its **algorithm**:

- **Round-robin** — hand requests out in turn, one server after another.
- **Least-connections** — send the next request to whichever server is least busy.
- **IP-hash** — always route a given client to the same server (useful when servers hold session state).

At the same time it runs **[[glossary:health-check|health checks]]** — small, repeated pings to each server. The instant a server stops responding, the balancer takes it out of rotation and stops sending it traffic, so users never land on a dead machine.

blocks.label: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 — what's the difference?
blocks.content: A **Layer 4** balancer routes on raw connection info (IP and port) — fast and simple, but blind to what the request contains. A **Layer 7** balancer reads the actual HTTP request, so it can route by URL path, headers, or cookies (e.g. send `/api` to one pool and `/images` to another). Layer 7 is more flexible; Layer 4 is lighter.

A single server has a hard ceiling — only so many CPUs, so much memory, so many open connections. Once you hit it, the only way up is *out*: run several servers and spread the load across them. But the moment you have more than one server, something has to decide who handles each request. That's the load balancer. It's the piece that makes [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]] actually work.

The load balancer also unlocks **zero-downtime operations**: because it can pull a server out of rotation, you can deploy new code or restart a machine one server at a time while the others keep serving traffic.

The catch is that the load balancer now sits in front of *everything*. If it goes down, your whole application is unreachable — so the thing you added for reliability becomes a **single point of failure** unless you make it redundant too (typically a standby balancer ready to take over).

Two more costs to weigh:

- **An extra hop** — every request passes through one more system, adding a little latency.
- **State gets awkward** — if a server remembers something about a user between requests, a round-robin balancer might send their next request to a *different* server that knows nothing about them.

Keep your servers **stateless** so any server can handle any request. If you can't, you're forced into *sticky sessions* (pinning a user to one server), which undercuts even balancing and breaks when that server dies. Push [[glossary:state|state]] into a shared store instead.

The load balancer sits between your clients and a fleet of [[glossary:server|servers]], and it's the linchpin of several other ideas. It depends on [[glossary:health-check|health checks]] to know which servers are alive, works with [[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]] and [[glossary:failover|failover]] to route around failures, and is what makes [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]] possible in the first place. In larger systems an [[glossary:api-gateway|API gateway]] often sits alongside it, adding auth and routing on top of plain load distribution.

blocks.caption: One entry point fans requests out across identical servers and skips any that fail their health check.

blocks.content: **NGINX** and **HAProxy** are the classic software load balancers you run yourself. In the cloud, managed options like **AWS ELB/ALB/NLB** and **Google Cloud Load Balancing** handle scaling and redundancy for you. **Envoy** is common inside microservice meshes. Even **DNS** can balance load at a coarse level by handing out different server addresses. Most large systems layer several: DNS spreading traffic across regions, then a load balancer spreading it across servers within each region.

quiz.scenario: It's Black Friday. Your single application server is pegged at 100% CPU and requests are timing out. You need more capacity, and you can't afford downtime.
quiz.question: What's the right move?

options.text: Put a load balancer in front and run several identical servers behind it.
options.explanation: This is horizontal scaling: spread the load across many servers through one entry point. You can also add and remove servers without downtime, which is exactly what a traffic spike needs.

options.text: Move the single server to a much bigger machine.
options.explanation: Vertical scaling buys time but still leaves one server — one ceiling and one point of failure. And resizing usually means a restart, i.e. downtime.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the database.
options.explanation: A cache helps if the database is the bottleneck. Here the application server's CPU is maxed, so reducing database reads won't free up the compute that's actually saturated.

options.text: Shard the database across several servers.
options.explanation: Sharding scales the database, not the application tier. The bottleneck is application CPU, which sharding doesn't touch.

shortDefinition: Adding more servers to handle increased traffic, rather than making a single server more powerful. Also called 'scaling out.'
analogy: When a coffee shop gets too busy, horizontal scaling means opening more locations across town rather than building a bigger shop. Each location shares the load of customers.

blocks.content: Horizontal scaling — “scaling out” — means handling more load by adding **more machines**, not by making one machine bigger. You run many copies of your application across a pool of servers and split the incoming work among them. Need more capacity? Add another server to the pool. Demand drops? Remove a few.

For this to work, something has to distribute requests across the pool and the servers have to be interchangeable:

- A **[[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]]** sits out front and sends each request to one of the servers.
- The servers are kept **stateless** — they hold no per-user memory between requests — so any server can handle any request.
- Shared data lives in a separate place (a database, a [[glossary:cache|cache]]) that all servers reach.

Done right, scaling becomes a knob you turn: add nodes to grow, remove them to shrink, often automatically.
The magic ingredient is **statelessness**. If a server remembers nothing about a user between requests, you can add and remove servers freely — because no single one is special.

Every single machine has a hard ceiling — only so many CPUs and so much memory exist in the biggest box you can buy. Once you hit that wall, [[glossary:vertical-scaling|making the machine bigger]] simply stops being an option. Scaling out has no such ceiling: you keep adding ordinary servers, and total capacity grows with each one.

It also brings **resilience** along for free. With many servers, the failure of one is survivable — the load balancer just stops sending it traffic and the rest carry on. A single big server, by contrast, is a single point of failure: when it dies, everything is down.

Horizontal scaling turns capacity into something **elastic**. You can match servers to demand hour by hour — spin up for the Black Friday rush, scale back down overnight — instead of paying for one giant machine sized for your worst case 24/7.

Many machines mean more moving parts. You now run a **distributed system**, and distributed systems are harder:

- **Coordination** — you need a load balancer, health checks, and a way to deploy to many servers at once.
- **State is the hard part** — anything a server needs to remember (sessions, uploads in progress) has to move into shared storage, or requests break when they land on a different server.
- **Operational overhead** — monitoring, logging, and debugging across a fleet is more work than babysitting one box.

Horizontal scaling only works if your application is built to be stateless. Bolt it onto an app that stores sessions or files locally on each server and users will hit confusing bugs — logged out at random, half-finished uploads vanishing — as their requests bounce between servers that don't share that state.

Horizontal scaling is the counterpart to [[glossary:vertical-scaling|vertical scaling]]: scale *out* by adding machines versus scale *up* by enlarging one. It's made possible by a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]], which spreads requests across the pool of [[glossary:server|servers]], and it leans on [[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]] — multiple servers mean one can fail without taking the system down.

Applied to data, horizontal scaling becomes [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] — splitting a database across servers instead of running one giant one. And it's a core reason teams adopt [[glossary:microservices|microservices]]: small, independent services can each be scaled out on their own, so you add capacity only where it's actually needed.

blocks.caption: Scaling out: a load balancer spreads traffic across identical servers.

blocks.content: Cloud platforms make scaling out routine: **AWS Auto Scaling Groups**, **Google Managed Instance Groups**, and **Kubernetes** add or remove servers (or containers) automatically based on CPU or request load. A load balancer like **AWS ELB** or **NGINX** sits in front. Stateless web tiers are the textbook case — run dozens of identical app servers and scale the fleet with traffic — while sessions and files are pushed into shared services like **Redis** or **S3** so no server holds anything unique.

quiz.scenario: Your web app already runs on the largest server your cloud provider offers, and traffic is still climbing. You can't make a single machine any bigger, and you need a path that keeps growing with demand.
quiz.question: What's the right approach?

options.text: Run multiple stateless servers behind a load balancer and add more as traffic grows.
options.explanation: This is horizontal scaling. Once you've hit the ceiling of a single machine, the only path that keeps growing is adding more servers and spreading load across them — with no fixed limit.

options.text: Move to an even more powerful single machine.
options.explanation: That's vertical scaling, and you've already maxed it out — there is no bigger machine. Scaling up has a hard ceiling that you've reached.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the database.
options.explanation: A cache helps when the database is the bottleneck. Here the app tier itself is out of capacity, and a single overloaded server stays overloaded no matter how fast its database reads are.

options.text: Shard the database across several servers.
options.explanation: Sharding scales the data tier, not the application tier. The constraint here is application compute on one maxed-out machine, which sharding doesn't address.

shortDefinition: Making a single server more powerful by adding more CPU, memory, or storage. Also called 'scaling up.' Simpler than horizontal scaling, but there's a ceiling on how big one machine can get.
analogy: Like replacing your home kitchen with a bigger one that has more counter space, a faster oven, and a larger fridge. It works well up to a point, but eventually you run out of room to expand.

blocks.content: Vertical scaling — “scaling up” — means handling more load by making your **single machine more powerful**. You don't add servers; you give the one you have more resources: more CPU cores, more RAM, faster disks, more network bandwidth. The application doesn't change — it just runs on a bigger box.

In the cloud this is often a one-line change: stop the instance, pick a larger size, start it again. Typical things you scale up:

- **CPU** — more cores for compute-heavy work.
- **Memory** — more RAM to hold bigger working sets or larger caches.
- **Disk** — faster SSDs and more capacity for I/O-bound workloads.

The appeal is simplicity: no load balancer, no distributing work, no rewriting the app — the same code, on more hardware.

Vertical scaling is the **simplest** way to get more capacity, and for many systems it's all you'll ever need. There's nothing distributed to manage: one machine means no coordination, no shared-state headaches, no extra moving parts. When you just need more headroom and fast, resizing one server beats re-architecting for many.

It's especially valuable for things that are genuinely hard to split across machines. A traditional [[glossary:relational-database|relational database]], for instance, is far easier to make bigger than to spread out — so the usual first move when a database strains is simply to give it a beefier box.

Start here. Squeeze everything you can out of a bigger machine before reaching for distributed approaches — vertical scaling is almost always cheaper in engineering effort, even if it costs more per server.

Scaling up runs into two unavoidable limits:

- **A hard ceiling** — there's a biggest machine money can buy, and once you reach it you're stuck. CPU and memory don't grow forever.
- **Single point of failure** — one machine means one thing to lose. If it goes down, everything goes down; there's no peer to take over.

It also tends to get **expensive non-linearly**: the top-end machine often costs far more than two mid-range ones with the same combined power.

Resizing usually means a **restart** — the machine goes down while it changes size. So the very moment you scale up to handle a surge, you may take a few minutes of downtime to do it. Plan vertical scaling for a maintenance window, not the middle of a traffic spike.

Vertical scaling is the natural counterpart to [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]]: scale *up* by enlarging one [[glossary:server|server]] versus scale *out* by adding many. They aren't either/or — most systems scale up first because it's simple, then scale out once they hit the single-machine ceiling or need the [[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]] that multiple machines provide.

The choice is sharpest for databases. Scaling a database up is easy but capped; the distributed alternatives — [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] and [[glossary:read-replica|read replicas]] — break through that cap but add real complexity. The common wisdom is to delay them by scaling up as long as you can.

On AWS, scaling up is picking a bigger EC2 instance type (an `m5.large` becomes an `m5.4xlarge`); the same idea applies to Google Cloud and Azure VM sizes. Managed databases like **Amazon RDS** let you bump the instance class with a few clicks. It's the default first response to a strained database or a single-server app — cheap in effort and effective right up until you hit the ceiling, at which point teams move to horizontal scaling, replicas, or sharding.

quiz.scenario: Your single-server relational database is starting to slow down under load. It's nowhere near the largest instance your cloud provider offers, and the app is a straightforward monolith you'd rather not re-architect right now.
quiz.question: What's the most pragmatic first move?

options.text: Resize the database to a larger instance with more CPU and memory.
