options.text: Add read replicas and route all reads to them.
options.explanation: Replicas help only if the pressure is read load. The scenario describes combined load from three feature areas including writes, which replicas can't relieve — every replica still applies all writes.

options.text: Vertically scale to a much larger single server.
options.explanation: A bigger box buys time but hits a ceiling, and it keeps three independent workloads contending on one machine. Splitting them by function is the more durable fix.

shortDefinition: In a distributed system you can't have perfect Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance all at once. Since network partitions are unavoidable, the real choice is consistency vs. availability when one happens.
analogy: Like two clerks at branch offices when the phone line between them dies. Either they refuse to update records until the line is back (staying in agreement), or they keep serving customers separately (staying open) and reconcile later. They can't do both.

blocks.content:
The CAP theorem describes a hard limit on any system that keeps copies of data on more than one machine. It names three properties:

- **Consistency (C)** — every read sees the most recent write, no matter which copy answers. This is [[glossary:strong-consistency|strong consistency]].
- **Availability (A)** — every request gets a (non-error) response, even if it might not reflect the very latest write.
- **Partition tolerance (P)** — the system keeps working even when the network between copies drops messages or splits into isolated groups.

The theorem says you can guarantee at most **two of the three** at the same time. But that framing is misleading on its own. In any real distributed system, the network *will* fail — cables get cut, switches reboot, a data center loses its link. A **partition** is not something you can opt out of, so **P is mandatory**. That collapses the choice into a single, concrete decision: *when a partition happens, do you sacrifice consistency or availability?*

blocks.label: So what does the choice actually look like during a partition?
blocks.content: Imagine two database replicas that can no longer talk to each other, and a write arrives at one of them. A **CP** system refuses to confirm the write (or refuses reads on the other side) because it can't guarantee the copies agree — it stays correct by becoming partly unavailable. An **AP** system accepts the write on both sides and keeps answering everyone, knowing the two sides have now diverged and must be reconciled once the link returns.

CAP matters because it forces an honest conversation that's easy to dodge until production. On a single server there is no CAP problem — one copy of the data is trivially consistent and the only failure is total. The moment you add a [[glossary:read-replica|replica]], a second region, or a distributed database for scale, you've signed up for partitions, and the theorem tells you that you must decide *in advance* what your system does when the network splits.

The decision is rarely all-or-nothing for a whole company — it's made **per piece of data**. Money, inventory, and seat counts usually demand consistency: it's better to show an error than to let two people buy the last item. Likes, feeds, comments, and presence indicators usually demand availability: it's better to show a slightly stale number than to go down. Naming this trade per feature is what separates a system that degrades gracefully from one that fails in surprising ways.

CAP only bites *during a partition*. When the network is healthy — which is most of the time — a well-built system can deliver both strong consistency and high availability. CAP is a statement about behavior under failure, not a permanent tax on every request.

A **CP** system chooses correctness over uptime. During a partition it returns errors or blocks rather than risk a stale or conflicting answer. You get data you can trust, but some users see failures until the network heals. This is the right call when a wrong answer is worse than no answer — financial ledgers, unique-username checks, the last seat on a flight.

An **AP** system chooses uptime over freshness. During a partition every side keeps accepting reads and writes, so nobody sees an outage — but the copies diverge, and you must reconcile them afterward (last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs). You trade temporary disagreement for staying online. This is the right call when being down costs more than being briefly stale — shopping carts, social feeds, telemetry.

CAP is **not** "pick any 2 of 3, permanently." You can't drop partition tolerance — the network decides that for you. And outside a partition you aren't forced to give up either C or A. The real, narrow statement is: *when a partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.* Treating it as a one-time menu of three is the classic misreading.

CAP is the failure-time view of the [[glossary:consistency|consistency]] spectrum. A **CP** system is leaning on [[glossary:strong-consistency|strong consistency]]: it would rather refuse a request than serve an out-of-date value. An **AP** system is embracing [[glossary:eventual-consistency|eventual consistency]]: it keeps serving and lets the copies converge once the partition clears. So the abstract C-vs-A choice in CAP is the same decision you make when you pick a consistency model for a specific piece of data.

It also connects directly to [[glossary:availability-nines|availability]]. Choosing AP is choosing to protect your uptime numbers during network trouble; choosing CP means accepting downtime in exchange for never being wrong. A more nuanced cousin, **PACELC**, extends CAP to say: during a Partition choose A or C, **Else** (when healthy) choose between Latency and Consistency — which is why even a fully connected system that wants strong consistency still pays a [[glossary:latency-vs-throughput|latency]] cost to coordinate.

Databases declare their lean. **CP-leaning** stores favor consistency under partition: **MongoDB** (with majority writes), **HBase**, **etcd**, **ZooKeeper**, and consensus-based systems like **Google Spanner** and **CockroachDB** will reject or block rather than serve divergent data. **AP-leaning** stores favor availability: **Cassandra**, **DynamoDB** (in its default mode), **Riak**, and **CouchDB** keep accepting requests during a partition and reconcile afterward.

Many modern systems are **tunable**, so CAP becomes a per-query setting rather than a fixed identity. Cassandra and DynamoDB let you ask for a quorum or strong read when correctness matters, and a fast one-replica read when availability matters. The practical takeaway: don't ask "is my database CP or AP?" — ask "for *this* operation, during a partition, do I want an error or a possibly-stale answer?"

quiz.scenario: Your e-commerce platform spans two data centers. The network link between them goes down for 90 seconds. During that window, customers in both regions keep browsing and adding items to their carts, and orders keep flowing.
quiz.question: For the checkout step that decrements the last unit of inventory, which CAP choice should that specific operation make during the partition?

options.text: Choose consistency (CP): refuse or block the final-inventory decrement until the copies can agree, even if some customers see an error.
options.explanation: Correct. Overselling the last unit is worse than a brief error, so this operation should sacrifice availability to stay consistent during the partition — the CP choice.

options.text: Choose availability (AP): let both regions sell the last unit and reconcile afterward.
options.explanation: AP keeps checkout up, but during a partition both regions could sell the same last unit, causing overselling. For scarce inventory, the stale-data risk of AP is exactly what you must avoid.

options.text: Drop partition tolerance so the question doesn't arise.
options.explanation: You can't drop partition tolerance — the network failed on its own. In a distributed system P is mandatory; CAP forces a choice between C and A, not the option to ignore partitions.

options.text: It doesn't matter; CAP only applies when the network is healthy.
options.explanation: The opposite is true. CAP's trade-off bites precisely *during* a partition; when the network is healthy a system can offer both consistency and availability.

shortDefinition: Latency is how long one operation takes; throughput is how many operations finish per unit of time. They measure different things and are often in tension — improving one can hurt the other.
analogy: Like a highway. Latency is how long it takes one car to drive from A to B. Throughput is how many cars pass a point per hour. A wider road moves far more cars per hour (high throughput) even if each individual car's trip isn't any faster.

blocks.content:
**Latency** is a *duration*: the time from starting a single operation to getting its result — a request's round trip, a query's run time, a page's load. It's measured in time units (milliseconds, microseconds) and answers "how long did *this one* take?"

**Throughput** is a *rate*: the number of operations the system completes in a window — requests per second, transactions per minute, megabytes per second. It answers "how *much* can the system get through?"

They're easy to conflate because both feel like "speed," but they're independent axes. A system can have low latency and low throughput (a single fast worker that can only do one thing at a time), or high latency and high throughput (a slow but massively parallel pipeline that finishes huge batches). Because latency varies request to request, throughput is usually reported as an average while latency is reported as **percentiles** — p50 (median), p95, p99 — since the slowest few requests are what users actually feel.

A rough mental model: **throughput ≈ concurrency ÷ latency**. If each request takes 100 ms (latency) and you can run 50 in parallel (concurrency), you finish about 500 per second (throughput). This is why you can raise throughput either by making each operation faster *or* by doing more of them at once.

Confusing the two leads to optimizing the wrong thing. If users complain the app feels *sluggish*, that's a **latency** problem — and adding more servers won't fix a single slow request. If the system *falls over under load* but each request is fine when it's quiet, that's a **throughput** problem — and shaving milliseconds off one request won't help it absorb the crowd.

Different goals need different fixes. You lower latency with [[glossary:cache|caching]], closer data ([[glossary:cdn|CDNs]]), faster algorithms, and fewer network hops on the critical path. You raise throughput with parallelism, batching, [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]], and [[glossary:async|asynchronous]] processing. Knowing which number is failing tells you which toolbox to open.

Users feel **latency**; operators budget for **throughput**. A great system optimizes the latency of the operations a human waits on, and the throughput of the firehose of work happening behind the scenes.

The two are often in direct tension, and **batching** is the clearest example. Grouping many small operations into one big one cuts per-item overhead and dramatically raises throughput — but each item now waits for the batch to fill up before it's processed, which raises that item's latency. A payment processor that flushes transactions once per second handles enormous volume, yet every individual transaction waits up to a second longer than if it were sent immediately.

The same trade shows up elsewhere:

- **Queues** smooth bursts and protect downstream systems (great for throughput and stability) but add waiting time to each item (worse latency).
- **Running near full capacity** maximizes throughput utilization, but queuing theory says latency spikes sharply as a system approaches 100% load.
- **Compression / bigger payloads** can move more data per second while making any single request take longer to assemble and ship.

Don't chase peak throughput by running your servers near 100% utilization. As a system approaches saturation, queue depths explode and **tail latency** (p99) goes through the roof — the system is technically "efficient" while feeling broken to real users. Leave headroom on purpose.

This trade-off is the engine behind several patterns. A [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]] is a throughput-and-resilience tool that deliberately accepts added latency: producers hand off work and move on, consumers drain the queue at their own pace, and bursts get absorbed instead of overwhelming the system. That's the [[glossary:async|asynchronous]] bargain — give up immediate, low-latency completion in exchange for higher sustained throughput.

On the latency side, a [[glossary:cache|cache]] is the canonical fix: serving from memory instead of disk or network turns a slow lookup into an instant one. And the whole distinction feeds into [[glossary:performance-vs-scalability|performance vs. scalability]] — latency is mostly a *performance* question (fast for one user), while sustaining throughput as load grows is mostly a *scalability* question (stays fast for many users).

Concrete numbers help anchor the intuition. Reading from memory takes ~100 nanoseconds; a round trip across a data center is ~0.5 ms; a round trip across the Atlantic is ~150 ms; a disk seek is several milliseconds. Those are **latency** facts no amount of scaling changes — which is why CDNs and caches exist to avoid the long trips entirely.

**Batching** trades latency for throughput everywhere: databases group writes into a single fsync, Kafka producers buffer messages (the `linger.ms` setting literally tunes how long to wait to build a bigger, higher-throughput batch), and GPUs process inference in batches to maximize utilization. The dial is explicit — a bigger batch or longer linger means more throughput and more per-item latency. Meanwhile latency-sensitive paths (a checkout button, an autocomplete dropdown) are tuned the opposite way: small payloads, no queuing, p99 watched like a hawk.

quiz.scenario: Your analytics service ingests billions of small events per day. Engineers add a step that buffers incoming events and writes them to the database in batches of 10,000 instead of one at a time. After the change, total events processed per second jumps sharply, but each individual event now takes a bit longer to show up in reports.
quiz.question: How best describes what the batching change did?

options.text: It raised throughput at the cost of per-event latency — the classic batching trade-off.
options.explanation: Exactly. Batching cuts per-item overhead so more events finish per second (higher throughput), but each event waits for its batch to fill, adding latency. The two metrics moved in opposite directions, which is the textbook tension.

options.text: It improved both latency and throughput at the same time.
options.explanation: Latency got worse, not better — each event now waits for its batch. The scenario explicitly says individual events take longer, so this isn't a free win on both axes.

options.text: It improved latency at the cost of throughput.
options.explanation: This is backwards. Batching raised throughput (more events per second) and hurt latency (each event slower), not the other way around.

options.text: It only changed scalability, leaving both latency and throughput unaffected.
options.explanation: Both metrics clearly changed — throughput rose and latency rose. Batching is precisely a latency-vs-throughput lever, not a no-op on those numbers.

shortDefinition: Performance asks "is it fast for a single user right now?" Scalability asks "does it stay fast as users and load grow?" They're different problems with different fixes.
analogy: Like a popular restaurant. Performance is how quickly one diner gets their meal on a quiet night. Scalability is whether the kitchen can still serve everyone in reasonable time when 300 people show up at once. A great chef (fast) can still run a kitchen that collapses under a crowd.

blocks.content:
**Performance** is about how a system behaves for a *single* unit of work in isolation: how fast one request completes when nothing else is competing for resources. It's largely a question of [[glossary:latency-vs-throughput|latency]] — the raw speed of the code path, the query, the round trip.

**Scalability** is about how that behavior *holds up as load increases*: more users, more requests, more data. A system is scalable if adding resources lets it handle proportionally more work without performance falling off a cliff.

The cleanest way to see the difference is to watch what happens to response time as load climbs:

- A system with **good performance but poor scalability** is fast at 1 user and grinds to a halt at 10,000 — every request fights over one shared resource.
- A system with **poor performance but good scalability** is mediocre at 1 user but stays *equally* mediocre at 10,000 — it spreads load cleanly, it just isn't tuned.
- The goal is **both**: fast for one user, and still fast for a million.

A useful definition: a system scales well if **performance stays roughly flat as you add load, provided you add resources**. If response time degrades even when you throw more hardware at it, you have a scalability problem — not a performance one.

Teams routinely solve the wrong problem because they don't separate these. A startup optimizes a function from 50 ms to 30 ms (a performance win) while the architecture still funnels every request through one database that will melt at launch (a scalability time bomb). Conversely, a team buys a huge cluster to "scale" when the real issue is one absurdly slow query — a performance fix that no amount of extra servers will paper over.

The fixes come from genuinely different toolboxes. **Performance** problems are solved by making the single path faster: better algorithms, [[glossary:cache|caching]], an [[glossary:index|index]] on the slow query, fewer network hops. **Scalability** problems are solved by changing the *shape* of the system so load can spread: [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]] behind a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]], [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] the data, removing shared bottlenecks. Diagnosing which one you have decides which path is even worth trying.

A blunt test: if the system is slow even with a single user, you have a **performance** problem. If it's fast with one user but degrades as users pile on, you have a **scalability** problem. The symptom ("it's slow") is the same; the cause and cure are not.

The trade-off is that the two goals can pull in opposite directions. The architectures that scale best often add overhead that *hurts* single-user performance. Splitting a fast [[glossary:monolith|monolith]] into [[glossary:microservices|microservices]] lets teams and load scale independently — but now one user's request hops across the network between services, so its latency goes *up*. Adding a [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]], a queue, or a replication layer all add a little distance to every request in exchange for the ability to grow.

Scaling strategy itself involves a trade. [[glossary:vertical-scaling|Vertical scaling]] (a bigger machine) often *improves* single-user performance and is dead simple, but it hits a hard ceiling and a single point of failure. [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|Horizontal scaling]] (more machines) has nearly unlimited headroom but forces you to handle distribution, coordination, and consistency — complexity that can slow the individual request down.

Don't reach for distributed, "web-scale" architecture before you need it. Premature scaling adds latency and operational complexity for load you don't have yet — often the result is a system that's *both* slow for your handful of real users and over-engineered. Make it fast for one user first; scale when the numbers actually demand it.

This pairing sits on top of [[glossary:latency-vs-throughput|latency vs. throughput]]: performance is mostly a latency story (one operation, fast), while scalability is mostly a throughput story (many operations per second, sustained as load grows). The two scaling approaches are the levers — [[glossary:vertical-scaling|vertical scaling]] tends to help performance, [[glossary:horizontal-scaling|horizontal scaling]] is the primary path to scalability.

Most scalability techniques are really about removing a shared bottleneck so load can spread. A [[glossary:load-balancer|load balancer]] spreads requests across many servers; [[glossary:sharding|sharding]] spreads data across many databases; a [[glossary:read-replica|read replica]] spreads read traffic. Each one is a scalability move, and several of them quietly cost a bit of per-request performance — which is exactly the tension this concept names.

A concrete contrast: suppose a report page runs a query that takes 4 seconds. That's a **performance** problem for every single user, and the fix is an [[glossary:index|index]], a rewritten query, or a cached result — adding servers does nothing because each one runs the same slow query. Now suppose each request is a snappy 50 ms but the single database maxes out its connections at 2,000 concurrent users. That's a **scalability** problem, and the fix is read replicas, a cache layer, or sharding so the load has somewhere to spread.

In real engineering you measure them separately. **Load testing** tools (k6, Locust, JMeter) plot response time against rising concurrent users — a flat line means it scales; an upward curve reveals the bottleneck. Single-request **profiling** (flame graphs, query `EXPLAIN` plans, traces) finds where one request spends its time. The mature workflow is: profile to make one request fast, then load-test to confirm it stays fast as the crowd arrives.

quiz.scenario: A dashboard loads in 300 ms when you're the only person testing it. But during the Monday-morning rush, when thousands of employees open it at once, load times climb to 15 seconds — even though each request, viewed alone, still does the same work. Adding a faster CPU to the single server barely helps.
quiz.question: What kind of problem is this, and what's the right class of fix?

options.text: A scalability problem — spread the load (horizontal scaling, replicas, caching the shared resource) so the system stays fast as users pile on.
options.explanation: Right. It's fast for one user and degrades as load grows, with a bigger CPU barely helping — the signature of a scalability bottleneck. The fix is changing the system's shape so load can spread, not tuning a single request.

options.text: A performance problem — profile and optimize the single request path to shave milliseconds.
options.explanation: Each request is already fast (300 ms) in isolation; the slowdown only appears under load. Micro-optimizing one fast request won't address a bottleneck that only shows up when thousands hit it at once.

options.text: A latency problem unrelated to load — add a CDN to cut network round trips.
options.explanation: Network latency wouldn't suddenly balloon from 300 ms to 15 s only during the rush. The trigger is concurrent load, which points to scalability, not a fixed per-request network cost a CDN would address.

options.text: There's no real problem; 15 seconds under peak load is unavoidable for any system.
options.explanation: It's very avoidable — that degradation under load is exactly what scalable architectures (replicas, caches, horizontal scaling behind a load balancer) are designed to prevent.

shortDefinition: A way to measure uptime as a percentage — "three nines" is 99.9%, "four nines" is 99.99%. Each extra nine shrinks your allowed downtime roughly tenfold and is far harder to reach.
analogy: Like a 24/7 convenience store advertising how rarely it's closed. "Open 99% of the year" still means dark doors for over three days. "99.99%" means under an hour all year. Every extra nine is a much bigger promise — and much more expensive to keep.

blocks.content: Availability is the share of time a system is up and serving requests, written as a percentage. Because the interesting differences live far out in the decimals, people count the **nines**: 99% is "two nines," 99.9% is "three nines," 99.99% is "four nines," 99.999% is "five nines." Each added nine cuts the allowed downtime by about **10×**.

The percentage only means something once you translate it into a **downtime budget** — how much outage it permits per year:

- **99% (two nines)** → ~3.65 days/year (~7.2 hours/month)
- **99.9% (three nines)** → ~8.77 hours/year (~43 minutes/month)
- **99.99% (four nines)** → ~52.6 minutes/year (~4.3 minutes/month)
- **99.999% (five nines)** → ~5.26 minutes/year (~26 seconds/month)

That budget is the right unit for planning: a single bad deploy can blow a whole year's three-nines allowance in one afternoon.

Quick conversion: downtime per year ≈ (1 − availability) × 525,600 minutes. So 99.9% → 0.001 × 525,600 ≈ 526 minutes ≈ 8.8 hours. Keep this handy — it turns an abstract percentage into a number you can actually budget against.

Nines turn a vague promise ("highly available") into a measurable, negotiable target. They're the language of **SLAs** (service-level agreements) — the uptime a vendor contractually owes, often with refunds if they miss it — and **SLOs**, the internal goals a team holds itself to. Stating a target as a number forces the real question: *how much downtime per year is acceptable, and what will it cost to get there?*

The cost curve is steep and nonlinear. Going from two nines to three might just need a [[glossary:health-check|health check]] and quick restarts. Three to four demands real [[glossary:redundancy|redundancy]] and automated [[glossary:failover|failover]]. Four to five means multi-region, no-single-point-of-failure architecture and rehearsed [[glossary:disaster-recovery|disaster recovery]] — often doubling cost and complexity for a few extra minutes of yearly uptime.

More nines isn't automatically better — it's a business decision. A blog at three nines is fine; a payment network at five nines is non-negotiable. The skill is matching the (expensive) target to what the product and its users actually require, not chasing nines for their own sake.

The headline trade-off is **cost and complexity per nine**. Each nine roughly multiplies the engineering effort: more redundant components, more automated failover, more regions, more monitoring, more on-call rigor. Past a point you're spending enormous sums to claw back minutes a year that your users may never notice.

The subtler trap is how availability **combines across components**, because it does *not* simply average:

- **In series (a dependency chain):** availabilities **multiply**, so the total is always *lower* than the weakest link. If a request must pass through three components each at 99.9%, overall availability is 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ **99.7%** — worse than any single piece.
- **In parallel (redundant copies):** you multiply the *failure* probabilities, so the total is *higher* than any single piece. Two redundant 99% components fail only if *both* fail: 1 − (0.01 × 0.01) = **99.99%**.

The classic mistake is assuming availability averages. Stacking nine services that are each "99.9%" in a dependency chain doesn't give you 99.9% — it gives ~99.1% (0.999⁹), because serial availabilities **multiply downward**. Every dependency you add on the critical path quietly *lowers* your ceiling. Redundancy raises it; serial dependencies erode it.

Nines are the *measurement*; the techniques that move the number are reliability patterns. [[glossary:redundancy|Redundancy]] is the foundation — parallel copies are precisely what makes combined availability go *up* instead of down. [[glossary:failover|Failover]] is how you actually collect on that redundancy fast enough to stay inside your downtime budget, and [[glossary:disaster-recovery|disaster recovery]] is the plan for the rare, large failures that threaten the most demanding nines.

Availability also sits on the other side of the [[glossary:cap-theorem|CAP]] trade-off: choosing **AP** (availability over consistency) during a partition is, quite literally, choosing to protect these nines at the risk of stale data, while choosing **CP** accepts downtime — and a dent in your availability number — to stay correct. The two are the same decision viewed through different lenses.

Cloud SLAs are stated in nines. A typical managed database or compute SLA promises **99.9%** or **99.99%**; premium multi-region configurations advertise higher. Note what an SLA *means*: it's a refund commitment, not a guarantee of zero downtime — at 99.99% the provider is openly telling you to expect up to ~52 minutes of outage a year. Reading the SLA tells you the downtime to design around.

The serial-multiplication math is why teams audit their **dependency chain**: if your service is 99.99% but it hard-depends on a third-party API at 99.9%, your real ceiling is ≈ 99.89% no matter how good your own code is. Practical responses are to remove non-essential dependencies from the critical path, add redundancy on the ones that remain, or apply [[glossary:graceful-degradation|graceful degradation]] so a flaky dependency degrades a feature instead of taking the whole system down. Google's SRE practice formalizes the budget side of this as an **error budget** — the allowed downtime is spent deliberately on releases and risk.

quiz.scenario: Your checkout service is rock-solid at 99.99% availability on its own. But to complete a purchase, every request must call three external dependencies in sequence — a tax API, a payment gateway, and a fraud-check service — each independently rated at 99.9% availability.
quiz.question: Roughly what end-to-end availability can checkout actually achieve, and why?

options.text: About 99.7% — serial dependencies multiply (0.9999 × 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997), so the chain is lower than its weakest link.
options.explanation: Correct. Components in series multiply their availabilities, pulling the total below every individual piece. Three 99.9% dependencies plus your own service land the chain near 99.7% — far short of your service's own 99.99%.

options.text: 99.99% — the service's own availability sets the ceiling regardless of its dependencies.
options.explanation: Dependencies on the critical path can only lower your effective availability, never raise it. Each serial call you must make multiplies in, so the weaker 99.9% dependencies drag the whole chain below 99.99%.

options.text: About 99.92% — average the four components' availabilities.
options.explanation: Availability in series doesn't average; it multiplies. Averaging overstates the result and misses the core point that every added serial dependency erodes the total.

options.text: Higher than 99.99% — chaining multiple services adds redundancy and improves uptime.
options.explanation: These services are in series (all required), not redundant. Redundancy (parallel copies of the *same* role) raises availability; required serial dependencies lower it.
